title: Low Back Pain Information on Austrian Healthcare Websites: Often Inaccurate, Biomedically Oriented, and Not Aligned With Clinical Guidelines-A Cross-Sectional Study
screen_reason: Systematic, population-wide content analysis of 125 official Austrian healthcare websites, assessed against the German national low back pain guideline, the JAMA benchmark and validated checklists. 76.8% (n = 96/125) were classified as 'mostly inaccurate' - a share of items in a sample judged inaccurate against an external ground truth (guideline concordance stated as accurate/inaccurate) with an explicit denominator, i.e. CONTENT prevalence. The authors themselves call the finding 'widespread misinformation'.

estimates.platform: Websites of official Austrian healthcare institutions (physiotherapy and medical practices, hospitals, national health agencies, medical universities)
estimates.date: Not stated in the abstract (cross-sectional website analysis; no data-collection window given)
estimates.measure_type: % of Austrian healthcare websites classified as mostly inaccurate on low back pain information
estimates.denominator: 125 official Austrian healthcare institution websites analysed in a systematic, population-wide website content analysis
estimates.definition: The website was classified as 'mostly inaccurate' when assessed with the JAMA benchmark, the German national low back pain guideline and validated checklists; the study explicitly assessed 'whether websites ... included inaccurate or misleading information'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "These findings highlight widespread misinformation and a lack of evidence-based communication on LBP across official Austrian healthcare websites." (the abstract offers no formal definition beyond inaccuracy relative to the national guideline)
estimates.source_quote: Using the JAMA benchmark, the German national LBP guideline, and validated checklists, we analysed 125 websites. Overall, 80.2% (n = 97/121) recommended at least one non-guideline-conform treatment; 76.8% (n = 96/125) were classified as mostly inaccurate.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Researcher assessment of each website against the German national low back pain guideline plus the JAMA benchmark and 'validated checklists'. Number of raters, coding rules for the 'mostly inaccurate' threshold and any inter-rater reliability are NOT reported in the abstract.
estimates.moderator_quote: We conducted a systematic, population-wide website content analysis in Austria to evaluate guideline adherence and the framing of LBP. Specifically, we assessed whether websites promoted guideline-concordant treatments, adopted a biomedical versus biopsychosocial perspective, and included inaccurate or misleading information.
estimates.notes: ABSTRACT-ONLY, several codings are inferences. year is left EMPTY: the abstract text gives neither a data-collection period nor a publication year, and the blindness rule forbids consulting any other file - an adjudicator should fill it from the record. classification_level=mixed because the checklist judgements are made on the content (claim-level) but the verdict 'mostly inaccurate' is assigned to the whole website (source-level); it is NOT a source-reliability list, so breadth is coded rather than left blank. sampling_frame=full_census follows 'systematic, population-wide'. population_scope=professional because the sampled units are institutional websites of healthcare professionals and agencies (an adjudicator could argue general_public on the grounds that the audience is patients). denom_scope=topical (a single clinical topic) with no rank truncation described, so denom_selection is empty. Note the two denominators differ (125 vs 121), meaning 4 websites were not evaluable for the treatment item.

estimates.platform: Websites of official Austrian healthcare institutions
estimates.measure_type: % of Austrian healthcare websites recommending at least one non-guideline-conform treatment for low back pain
estimates.denominator: 121 of the 125 Austrian healthcare websites (the 4-website shortfall is not explained in the abstract)
estimates.definition: The website recommended at least one treatment that is not concordant with the German national low back pain guideline.
estimates.misinfo_def: "These findings highlight widespread misinformation and a lack of evidence-based communication on LBP across official Austrian healthcare websites."
estimates.source_quote: Overall, 80.2% (n = 97/121) recommended at least one non-guideline-conform treatment; 76.8% (n = 96/125) were classified as mostly inaccurate.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Assessment of guideline concordance of the recommended treatments against the German national low back pain guideline; no raters or reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Using the JAMA benchmark, the German national LBP guideline, and validated checklists, we analysed 125 websites.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL: coded QUALITY, not CONTENT. Recommending a treatment that is not guideline-concordant is a guideline-ADHERENCE judgement, and a website could state something wholly true (e.g. accurately describing a therapy) and still be counted in this numerator - which is the protocol's trigger for QUALITY plus borderline=true. The 76.8% 'mostly inaccurate' row above is the accuracy-based (CONTENT) figure. Note also that this row's denominator (121) differs from the accuracy row's (125), so the two are not nested variants of one another and definition_variant is left false.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED: (1) '85.6% of websites adopting this perspective' (biomedical rather than biopsychosocial framing) - a framing/orientation measure, not truth or falsity, and the abstract gives no denominator count for it. (2) The JAMA benchmark scores themselves are not reported numerically. (3) The abstract gives no data-collection dates, no publication year, no number of raters, no reliability statistic, no definition of the 'mostly inaccurate' threshold, and does not explain the 125 vs 121 denominator difference - all of which limit confidence and are unrecoverable from the abstract alone. (4) No breakdown by website type (practice vs hospital vs agency vs university) is given, so no sub-rows are derivable.

rob.design: Cross-sectional, self-described 'systematic, population-wide' content analysis of 125 official Austrian healthcare institution websites (physiotherapy/medical practices, hospitals, national health agencies, medical universities), assessed with the JAMA benchmark, the German national LBP guideline and validated checklists for guideline-concordant treatment recommendation, biomedical vs biopsychosocial framing, and inaccurate/misleading information. Abstract-only: no search or collection dates, no inclusion/exclusion procedure, no number of assessors, no inter-rater reliability, no threshold definition for 'mostly inaccurate', and an unexplained denominator difference (97/121 vs 96/125).
